summary: Redwood demo focused on using the model catalog and Optimize recommendations to pick an open model for Bluebridge's customer-service summarization pipeline. Covered latency/cost tradeoffs, compatibility matrix for GPU/quant profiles, and securing dedicated vs hosted deployment. Agreed to run a short bench pilot with customer payloads and exchange security artifacts.
topics: deployment mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private)
transcript:
[00:00] Avery Lewis: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. We scheduled 50 minutes to walk through a practical selection demo — how to pick an open model from the catalog, interpret benches, and make a pragmatic tradeoff decision for latency and cost. Samir and June are with me from engineering.
[00:20] Maya Chen: Thanks, appreciated. We want to get from exploration to a pilot quickly — main constraints are 99th perc latency under 400ms for short chitchat responses, and budget target roughly $0.0008 per token equivalent. We'll also need SOC2 and VPC controls.
[00:40] Samir Patel: Got it. Quick clarifying Q: when you say 400ms, is that median or p99?
[00:45] Maya Chen: P99 is critical. Median can be lower.
[00:50] June Park: Great — we'll show the catalog filters for latency profile then the Optimize suggestions (batching, quant) and how to map to dedicated GPUs or hosted.
[01:10] Luis Ortega: Also worth calling out we run on GCP us-west and prefer spare capacity there. If you have region constraints that matters.
[01:20] Avery Lewis: Noted. Quick agenda slide — 1) catalog shortlist 2) bench reading 3) compatibility matrix to hardware/quant 4) deployment options and SSO/KMS notes 5) next steps.
[01:35] Tom Reed: Sounds good.
[02:00] June Park: Jumping into the console, on the left is model catalog. We'll filter to "open models" and set the cost/latency slider to show candidates under our baseline. A couple that often show up for summarization are: a smaller 7B quantized variant for edge throughput, a 13B int8 variant that balances quality, and a 30B float16 that gives best quality but higher latency.
[02:35] Samir Patel: Important nuance — the catalog also shows a compatibility column: which kernels were validated (triton/flash attention/llamattx) and whether quantized paths are available for the family. The compatibility matrix is our quick heuristic to know if a model will hit your latency target on X hardware.
[03:05] Maya Chen: Can you show how you interpret bench numbers? We saw a spreadsheet earlier but numbers were confusing.
[03:12] Samir Patel: Sure. Example row: model A (13B-int8) — median latency 120ms at batch 1, p95 280ms, tokens/sec stable at 350 on a T4-equivalent baseline. But that T4 baseline maps poorly to your p99 needs; we recommend testing on an A10/A100 class or using Dedicated + autoscale.
[03:45] Luis Ortega: We don't have A100 in prod; that's expensive. We were thinking N4-standard or T4 in GCP.
[03:52] June Park: That's common. Optimize can suggest quant and kernel settings that make a 13B-int8 run very close to your p99 if you accept a small quality delta. There's also KV cache and prefix caching options for repeated prompts to cut token work.
[04:12] Maya Chen: About quality delta — how do you measure it? We care about summary fidelity and hallucination rate.
[04:18] Samir Patel: We run automated evals (ROUGE-ish + targeted QA checks) plus a small human eval sample. In the catalog each model has a 'bench signal'—a combined score weighted by latency, cost, and accuracy for common tasks. But it's a starting point.
[04:40] Tom Reed: Can you run an example mapping? Pick two candidates and show the matrix to our hardware.
[04:45] June Park: Yep. Picking Candidate X (13B int8) and Candidate Y (7B q4_0). In the compatibility matrix: X shows validated int8 kernels for A10 + A100 and an estimated p99 at 350ms on an A10 with single-request config; on T4 it's over 700ms at p99. Y on T4 is ~220ms p99 but lower ROUGE on long-form summaries.
[05:20] Maya Chen: So the tradeoff is: pick 7B to hit latency but lose some summary accuracy; pick 13B and need stronger GPUs. Is that accurate?
[05:28] Samir Patel: Exactly. You can also do a hybrid routing policy — e.g., serve short responses on 7B and longer/higher-quality flows on 13B, or use A/B for a subset of traffic.
[05:40] Luis Ortega: Hybrid sounds interesting. How much ops overhead is that?
[05:44] Avery Lewis: Our Console has routing rules and Canary/A/B rollout support — you can set per-route model policies and automatic fallback. We can show a route where short-summary endpoint maps to 7B with cache, and fallback to 13B for edge cases.
[06:08] Tom Reed: What's the developer experience like — SDK, latency instrumentation?
[06:12] Samir Patel: SDKs are idiomatic. Dedicated plus Console gives tracing and token-level cost breakdown. Optimize also suggests batch sizes, KV cache TTL, and when to use streaming to reduce perceived latency.
[06:28] Maya Chen: Can you walk through an actual bench run? What's needed from us?
[06:33] June Park: We typically ask for 3 representative prompt sets and expected QPS. Samir will provide a bench template. We'll run against a few model variants on our hosted infra or your dedicated pool, and return a CSV with median/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and cost estimate.
[06:52] Luis Ortega: If we run on our infra, what do you need access to? We prefer not to share data.
[06:57] Samir Patel: For private, we package a bench container that runs locally and emits results to a customer-only S3 bucket or returns CSVs you upload. No customer payload leaves your VPC unless you opt into hosted runs. For hosted runs we'd need scrubbed samples.
[07:18] Priya Nair: Security here is key. How do you handle keys, KMS, audit logs?
[07:23] Avery Lewis: We support customer KMS for Private, HSM integrations on Dedicated for enterprise, SSO/SAML for console access, RBAC at the route and token granularity, and audit logs — we can provide examples. We'll attach SOC2 docs and an architecture note in the follow-up.
[07:40] Priya Nair: Good. Also need data retention policy and ability to disable logs for certain routes.
[07:45] June Park: You can control retention per-route, and there's a 'no-logs' mode for sensitive endpoints. We'll document that.
[07:55] Maya Chen: Back to the catalog: can you create a custom shortlist for our workload?
[07:58] Samir Patel: Yes — we can create a shortlist with weighted signals (latency importance 0.6, quality 0.4) and produce an ordered picklist. Then run bench candidates.
[08:12] Tom Reed: Show us an example shortlisting UI please.
[08:18] June Park: (screen) here's the picklist UI — you can drag models, add weightings, and preview estimated cost per 1M tokens under different batch assumptions. Notice the 'compatibility heatmap' at right: green means validated kernels and quant path, yellow is partial, red means we recommend caution.
[08:45] Maya Chen: I see Candidate Z is yellow — what does partial mean?
[08:48] Samir Patel: Partial means some kernels validated but not the int8 path on the exact sequence lengths you care about. We can run a focused kernel mapping to see if there's a path for you.
[09:05] Luis Ortega: Kernel mapping — is that something we run or you run?
[09:09] Samir Patel: We run it with your sample payloads. It will test attention kernels and fallbacks and show where latency stems from. Usually takes a day.
[09:18] Maya Chen: Are fallback policies automatic if a kernel isn't present?
[09:22] June Park: At runtime the serving runtime will use the compatible kernel or fall back to float path. The Console's routing can prefer quantized variants and fallback to non-quant when necessary.
[09:35] Tom Reed: Is there support for mixed precision?
[09:37] Samir Patel: Yes — mixed precision paths are available for many models. The catalog shows whether we've validated mixed precision kernels. It's another knob between cost and quality.
[09:45] Maya Chen: Practical question — we are constrained by a hard spend cap per month. What levers do you recommend first?
[09:52] Avery Lewis: Order of levers: 1) Choose smaller model family if quality acceptable 2) Quantize (int8/q4) 3) Use prefix/KV caching to cut tokens 4) Smart routing (short responses on cheaper models) 5) Reserved capacity for price predictability. Optimize will compute unit economics estimates for you.
[10:20] Luis Ortega: How accurate are those cost estimates? We need to justify to finance.
[10:23] June Park: Estimates are conservative; we model token composition and typical batching. We can also provide a delta if you pick dedicated vs hosted. For reserved capacity, we'll show effective per-token cost.
[10:40] Maya Chen: Demo the Optimize suggestion flow.
[10:43] Samir Patel: (screen) In Optimize you upload a sample set or pick a route. The tool runs heuristics and suggests batch sizes, cache TTLs, and model variant. It will say: expected token cost $X, expected p99 latency Y. You can then accept to apply to route or export runbook.
[11:10] Tom Reed: A question about rollout: if we apply a quant suggestion in production, how do we detect quality regressions?
[11:16] June Park: We integrate evals into rollouts — when you apply a change, we run a small A/B with automatic quality checks (ROUGE, semantic-similarity) and alert if quality drops beyond a threshold. You can auto-rollback.
[11:30] Maya Chen: Great. Can we control the sample size for the eval?
[11:33] Samir Patel: Yes, that's configurable.
[11:40] Luis Ortega: Any limits on concurrent models per route?
[11:43] Avery Lewis: No hard limit — Console and routing support many variants. Ops complexity grows but the UI and API expose that.
[11:55] Tom Reed: One more enterprise question: If we pick Dedicated, is there an option to restrict internet egress for the model containers?
[12:02] Samir Patel: For Private and Dedicated we support VPC-only setup and private control plane options. For fully air-gapped, we have an on-prem package with audit controls. We'll send the deployment architecture doc.
[12:20] Maya Chen: Good. Back to the bench: can you show a sample bench CSV and how to read cost columns?
[12:25] June Park: (screen) CSV columns: model, variant, hw, batch, median_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, tokens_per_sec, est_cost_per_1M_tokens, quality_score. We highlight rows meeting your latency/cost constraints.
[12:50] Samir Patel: Example: 13B-int8 on A10 — p99 380ms, est_cost $0.0012/1k tokens. 7B-q4 on T4 — p99 220ms, est_cost $0.0007/1k tokens, quality delta 6%.
[13:10] Maya Chen: That delta is borderline for us. If we run a small human eval, how long to get reliable signal?
[13:18] June Park: For quality on summaries, 100–200 samples with two raters is usually enough to surface big regressions.
[13:28] Luis Ortega: Operationally, what's the simplest pilot to prove fit?
[13:31] Samir Patel: Run a 1-week bench: Redwood runs inference on your sample set across 3 variants (7B-q4, 13B-int8, 13B-fp16), produce latency + cost CSVs, and run automated evals. If you want, do the run on your infra with our bench container.
[13:48] Maya Chen: Let's do that. We'll send prompts.
[13:50] Tom Reed: On procurement side, any minimums for Dedicated?
[13:54] Avery Lewis: Dedicated has reserved capacity options — monthly commitments. We can propose a pilot pricing model for the bench period with no long-term commitment.
[14:05] Priya Nair: One more on compliance: do you provide contract language around data residency?
[14:10] June Park: Yes — we have data residency clauses and can include DPA addendum. We'll attach templates.
[14:20] Maya Chen: Okay, let's outline the pilot timeline and responsibilities.
[14:23] Avery Lewis: Proposed timeline: Day 0–2 collect prompts + QPS; Day 3 run bench; Day 4 review results + small human eval; Day 5 produce recommendation and route config. We can stretch to a week if you want more samples.
[14:40] Luis Ortega: Works. Who needs to do what?
[14:43] Avery Lewis: We'll capture action items — send security docs (us), bench runbook (Samir), sample prompts + traffic patterns (you).
[15:00] Maya Chen: Good. Two technical follow-ups: 1) can you show kernel mapping summary after the bench? 2) is there a way to simulate p99 under peak bursts?
[15:10] Samir Patel: Yes — kernel map comes after bench artifacts. For burst p99 we'll run stress runs and include tail-latency traces. We also have suggestions for autoscale buffer sizing.
[15:30] Tom Reed: Are there any gotchas we should watch for with quantized 13B models on T4?
[15:35] Samir Patel: Two gotchas: memory fragmentation leading to occasional OOMs at high concurrency, and some attention kernel slow paths for long sequences. Both are visible in kernel mapping and we have mitigations (mem pool tuning, sequence chunking).
[15:55] Maya Chen: Great. Any competitors differentiators we should call out?
[16:00] Avery Lewis: Quick: Vertex AI integrates well but is more heavyweight; SageMaker is broad but less tuned for dynamic fallback and unit-cost tooling; Run:AI focuses on cluster scheduling. Our differentiator is integrated Optimize + Console with production-grade fallbacks and per-route economics.
[16:25] Luis Ortega: Thanks. Let's move to questions from the team.
[16:30] Speaker 6: Are there limits to the eval metrics you surface? Can we add custom checks?
[16:35] June Park: You can plug custom evals — e.g., hallucination detectors or domain-specific QA. We'll include the eval integration doc.
[16:45] Maya Chen: One small nit — the Console UI seemed to surface a lot of candidate variants. How do you prevent combinatorial explosion of routes?
[16:53] Samir Patel: We encourage a constrained shortlist and use runtime policies to collapse variants behind strategy groups. We'll help design a simple routing plan for the pilot.
[17:10] Tom Reed: For billing, how visible is cost per route?
[17:14] Avery Lewis: Console gives per-route token and dollar spend down to the token. For Dedicated reserved commits, we show amortized token cost after commitment.
[17:30] Maya Chen: Good. Any final demos to wrap up?
[17:33] June Park: Quick demo of applying an Optimize suggestion to a route: choose route, preview expected delta, run A/B with 10% traffic, auto-check quality, then promote. (screen) preview shows p99 360ms, est_cost per 1M tokens $X.
[17:58] Samir Patel: I'll also show the compatibility matrix export — it highlights validated kernels and suggests hardware.
[18:10] Maya Chen: That looks actionable. We'll send the sample prompt sets tonight.
[18:15] Luis Ortega: One last ops Q: if we discover a regression after rollout, what's the rollback time?
[18:20] June Park: Immediate. The route rollback is instant and traffic shifts within seconds; config propagation depends on your edge but typically sub-30s.
[18:30] Tom Reed: Perfect.
[18:35] Maya Chen: Thank you, team.
[18:38] Avery Lewis: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with security docs and bench runbook.
[18:45] (call ends)
